title: Is Protecting Someone from Every Consequence Really Love?
deck: The best protection does not shut out every consequence. It helps someone become better able to understand, choose, and bear what follows.
body: When we love someone, we naturally hope they will suffer a little less harm.

When we see them making a mistake, we want to warn them in advance; when difficulty approaches, we want to move it aside; once they have fallen, we want to pick up the pieces as quickly as possible and restore life to the way it was.
Protection thus easily comes to seem like something of which more is always better.
If pain can be avoided, why not avoid it? If we can bear it for them, why watch them suffer?
But the consequences someone experiences are not all bad things that can simply be deleted from life.

Some consequences also tell them what their choices have affected, what they have overlooked, and where the limits of their capacity lie. They reconnect action with the world, making a decision more than a thought that has passed through the mind.
When someone else absorbs every consequence, this connection grows weaker and weaker.

A person can make decisions again and again yet rarely encounter the weight they bring. A plan fails, and someone immediately makes up for it; a promise goes unfulfilled, and someone explains on their behalf; resources are exhausted, and someone replenishes them. Every difficulty is solved, but it becomes harder and harder for them to know what their choices actually mean.
Here, protection changes.
It no longer merely prevents an injury. It also begins to bear for someone the part of reality that belongs to the formation of their own judgment.
This does not mean that suffering has value in itself, still less that loving someone means making them suffer.

Some consequences are so severe that a single occurrence can destroy the capacity to choose again in the future. Approaching danger, irreversible harm, and risks far beyond what someone can bear may all require timely intervention. Great harm that can be prevented should not be allowed to happen for the sake of supposedly “learning a lesson.”
The distinction we really need is not between protecting and not protecting, but between the directions protection takes.
One kind of protection asks only: how can I keep them from hurting this time?
Another also asks: after this help, will they be better able to see risks, make decisions, and bear the consequences?
The first may take over more and more. The second looks for places where it can step back.

Suppose, for example, someone makes a choice they have not thought through sufficiently. You can help them avoid the most serious losses while involving them in putting things right; you can offer resources while making their limits clear; you can face the outcome alongside them without explaining for them to everyone or rewriting the responsibility as something that has nothing to do with them.
Such protection does not leave someone alone in difficulty, nor does it make that difficulty disappear entirely into someone else’s life.
It preserves an important fact: this is a situation they have helped to create, and one they can help to change.
Sometimes we treat bearing everything for someone else as proof of deeper love.

But bearing things without limit can also quietly change a relationship. One person grows more accustomed to being caught, while the other increasingly believes that without them, the person could not live.
Both may find a kind of security in this arrangement.

The protected person does not have to face all the uncertainty, and the protector acquires an irreplaceable place. Over time, help no longer aims at making the other person more capable, but at keeping this dependence in place.
This need not be something either person has brought about deliberately.
Love and need become entangled easily. We want to matter, and we fear that when the other person no longer needs us, the relationship will become less secure.
So, even while solving the problem, we may preserve a condition that keeps us needed.
Real protection, however, must allow another outcome:
One day, the other person can handle alone what they once needed you to handle. They no longer consult you at every step or feel uneasy without your approval.
This does not mean that your help has lost its meaning. On the contrary, it may show that the help has accomplished its hardest part.
Protecting someone does not mean keeping them under your protection forever.
Of course, there are shared consequences in relationships as well.

If someone’s choices repeatedly pass debt, risk, care responsibilities, or the consequences of broken trust on to others, they cannot shut down discussion simply by saying, “Let me bear my own consequences.” Others have the right to refuse to serve as an endless buffer and to change how far they are willing to remain involved.
Letting someone face consequences does not mean looking on coldly; refusing to clear away every consequence is not necessarily punishment, either.
Sometimes it simply restores reality to its proper place: whoever makes a decision should share in bearing it; whoever will be affected also has the right to state their limits.
Love is not about guaranteeing that another person will never fall.

It reaches out when devastating harm can be prevented, offers company through ordinary difficulties, and, when the other person can stand, does not keep holding them in the position of someone who must be supported.
The best protection does not keep life from ever touching someone again.
It enables them, when life really does touch them, still to understand, choose, revise, and stand up again.
entry_door: This essay uses no theoretical terms, but behind it lies the same question: how can a relationship draw close to someone without living their life for them? To follow this line of thought further, start with Non Dubito in Five Minutes.
